## 🧩 The mystery

It is your very first day. Prof. Zola waves you toward an empty desk with a
laptop on it and says one thing:

> "Get set up. We start real work tomorrow."

Then she is gone.

Amina (that is you) sits down. No pipettes. No reagents. No bench. Just a
laptop and a blinking cursor. And a small, honest question: set up *what*,
exactly?

Here is the thing nobody tells you on day one. A wet-lab scientist does not
start an experiment by grabbing the first tube in sight. They set up their
bench first. Clean surface. Tips in the rack. Reagents labelled. Only then do
they start.

You are about to do the same. The only difference is that yours is a **dry lab**
bench, made of software instead of glassware. (Wet lab means the physical bench
with pipettes and reagents. Dry lab means the computational one.) Get it right
once, and every experiment in every module after this just works.

::: {.think}
Most bioinformatics tools are written for Unix, a family of operating systems
that includes Linux and macOS. Windows is not Unix.

So before you install a single tool, ask: does your computer even speak the
right language yet? **Yes? No? Not sure?** Hold that thought. We will sort it
out together, one small step at a time.
:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" collapse="true"}
## A gentle word before we begin (read if you are nervous)

If you have ever opened a "beginner" tutorial and met a wall of cryptic
commands on line one, welcome. You are among friends, and that is *not*
happening here.

This module is the least glamorous part of bioinformatics. Nobody grows up
dreaming of installing a package manager. But it quietly decides whether
everything *after* it goes smoothly or turns into a week of mysterious errors.
Getting it right once saves you a genuinely enormous amount of pain later.

Three honest things to set expectations:

- **This is a guided tour, not the whole map.** These tutorials get you moving
  and show you the lay of the land. Real comfort takes *your* effort too:
  reading the official docs, experimenting, looking things up when stuck. We
  point you to good sources along the way.
- **You learn this by doing, not reading.** Type the commands yourself. Hitting
  an error is not failure, it *is* the work. Every bioinformatician you admire
  has squinted at a baffling error message today.
- **Go at your own pace.** No points for speed, nobody is timing you. When a
  step misbehaves, take a breath. The **Verify** and **Troubleshooting** notes
  exist precisely because you are not the first person to trip there.

One small step at a time, and you will be fine. Let us build your bench.
:::

## Your path through this module

Four small steps. The first one depends on your operating system; the rest are
the same for everyone. You can follow the progress outline on the side as you go.

::: {.cba-modsteps}
1. **Get a Unix shell** &nbsp;·&nbsp; the environment every tool expects
2. **Install Conda** &nbsp;·&nbsp; your package and environment manager
3. **Configure channels and build your first environment** &nbsp;·&nbsp; the bench gets its tools
4. **Make it reproducible** &nbsp;·&nbsp; save an environment you can rebuild anywhere
:::

By the end you will have a working Unix command line, Conda installed via
Miniforge, the Bioconda and conda-forge channels configured, and your first
isolated environment with real tools in it, plus the skill to recreate it from a
file. This is the foundation for every other module. Take your time.

::: {.story}
Picture a chemistry bench. The reason a scientist keeps reagents in labelled,
separate bottles (and not all sloshed into one bucket) is simple: if project A
uses one buffer and project B needs another, mixing them ruins both.

Software is the same. Tools have versions, and versions clash. Conda gives you
labelled bottles for software, called **environments**, so project A's tools
never break project B's. That is the whole reason we bother with all this setup.
:::

::: {.callout-warning collapse="true"}
## Before you start: prerequisites and a word on versions

**Windows:** Windows 10 (version 2004 or newer) or Windows 11, with
administrator rights.

**macOS:** a reasonably recent macOS. Note whether your Mac has an **Apple
Silicon** chip (M-series) or an **Intel** chip; it matters in Step 3. Check via
the **Apple menu → About This Mac**.

**Everyone:** a stable internet connection, a few GB of free disk space, and
comfort with copy-pasting commands and reading the output carefully.

Every version number below (Ubuntu release, Miniforge, tool versions) is an
**example at the time of writing**. Installation methods for WSL and Conda have
changed before and may change again. When a step matters, confirm it against the
official source. If a command behaves differently than described, trust the
official docs over this tutorial.
:::

---

## Step 1 · Get a Unix shell {#step-1}

Bioinformatics tools speak Unix. This step gets you a real Unix command line.
**Pick your operating system below.** You only need your own tab.

::: {.panel-tabset}

### 🪟 Windows

Your Windows machine speaks one language, and bioinformatics tools speak Unix.
Instead of wiping Windows, you open a small, fully functional Ubuntu Linux
"embassy" inside it using **WSL (Windows Subsystem for Linux)**. WSL2 runs a
genuine Linux kernel and is what you want.

#### Check your Windows version

- Press `Windows key + R`, type `winver`, press Enter.
- You want **Windows 10 version 2004 (build 19041) or higher**, or **Windows 11**.

If you are on an older build, update Windows first (Settings → Windows Update)
before continuing.

#### Install WSL and Ubuntu

Open **PowerShell as Administrator** (click Start, type `PowerShell`, right-click
**Windows PowerShell**, choose **Run as administrator**), then run:

```powershell
wsl --install
```

On a supported, up-to-date Windows this single command enables the required
features and installs the **default Ubuntu** distribution. **Reboot when
prompted.** After rebooting, Ubuntu often finishes setup automatically and opens
a terminal window.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Optional: choose a specific Ubuntu version
```powershell
wsl --list --online          # see available distributions
wsl --install -d Ubuntu-22.04 # install a specific one (confirm the exact name)
```
For teaching, stick with a recent **LTS** (Long-Term Support) release, since
tutorials and tools target LTS. Which release is "current LTS" changes over
time; check ubuntu.com if unsure.
:::

#### First launch: create your Linux user

The first time Ubuntu starts, it asks for a **UNIX username and password**.

- This user is **separate** from your Windows account.
- When typing the password, **nothing appears on screen**. That is normal Linux
  behavior, not a frozen terminal. Type it and press Enter.
- Remember this password: you need it for `sudo` (administrator) commands.

#### Update the package lists

Inside your new Ubuntu terminal:

```bash
sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade -y
```

`sudo` runs as administrator (it asks for the Linux password you just set), `apt`
is Ubuntu's system package manager, and `-y` auto-confirms.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## ✅ Check: did it work?
It finished without red `E:` error lines. Confirm your Ubuntu version with:
```bash
lsb_release -a
```
Expected (yours will differ):
```
Distributor ID: Ubuntu
Description:    Ubuntu 22.04.x LTS
```
:::

#### Where are my files? (Windows ↔ Linux)

This trips up almost everyone. Think of two rooms connected by a narrow doorway:

- Your **Windows** drives appear inside Linux under `/mnt/`. Your `C:\` drive is
  at `/mnt/c/`, so Downloads is roughly `/mnt/c/Users/<YourWindowsName>/Downloads`.
- Your **Linux home** directory is `~` (that is `/home/<your-linux-user>`).
- From Windows, browse Linux files by typing `\\wsl$\` in File Explorer's address bar.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Performance tip that matters a lot
Keep your **analysis project files inside the Linux filesystem** (for example in
`~`), **not** under `/mnt/c/...`. Crossing the Windows/Linux boundary for many
files is noticeably slower and causes permission headaches. Treat `/mnt/c` as a
place to copy files in and out, not to run pipelines from.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Optional: nicer tools
- **Windows Terminal** (from the Microsoft Store): tabs and better fonts for WSL.
- **VS Code + the "WSL" extension**: edit files and run the terminal inside your
  Linux environment. From Ubuntu, launch it in the current folder with `code .`
  (the first time, VS Code installs a small helper into WSL).
:::

::: {.callout-warning collapse="true"}
## 🧰 Troubleshooting (Windows)
- **`wsl --install` is not recognized** → your Windows is likely too old, or you
  are not in PowerShell. Update Windows; use PowerShell (not Command Prompt) as
  Administrator.
- **Virtualization error / WSL2 will not start** → virtualization may be disabled
  in your BIOS/UEFI, or the "Virtual Machine Platform" Windows feature is off.
  This is firmware specific; consult Microsoft's official WSL troubleshooting
  page for your machine.
- **Forgot your Linux password** → it can be reset, but the procedure differs by
  setup; look up the current official method rather than an old forum command.
- **`wsl --install` still errors** → the command is defined by Microsoft and has
  changed across Windows updates. Search Microsoft's official "Install WSL" docs
  for your exact Windows version.
:::

### 🍎 macOS

Good news: macOS is built on a Unix foundation, so, unlike Windows, you **do not
need WSL**. You already have a real Unix shell. There are just a few things to
set up so bioinformatics tools install cleanly. Your bench is half built already.

#### Open the Terminal

- Press `Cmd + Space`, type `Terminal`, press Enter.
- Modern macOS uses **`zsh`** as the default shell (older versions used `bash`).
  Everything here works in either; occasionally you will see a note where they
  differ.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## ✅ Check: which shell am I in?
```bash
echo $SHELL
```
Prints something ending in `zsh` or `bash`, for example `/bin/zsh`.
:::

#### Install the Command Line Developer Tools

These provide essentials like `git`, `curl`, and compilers that many tools expect:

```bash
xcode-select --install
```

A dialog pops up. Click **Install** and accept the license. If it says the tools
are *already installed*, you are good.

#### Know your chip: Apple Silicon vs Intel

This is the one Mac-specific thing that genuinely affects bioinformatics, so note
it now:

```bash
uname -m
```

Expected output, one of:

```
arm64     # Apple Silicon (M-series)
x86_64    # Intel
```

**Why it matters:** historically, some Bioconda packages were built for Intel
Macs (`osx-64`) but not yet for Apple Silicon (`osx-arm64`). We handle this in
[Step 3's Apple Silicon note](#apple-silicon-note). For now, just know which chip
you have.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Optional: Rosetta 2 (running Intel software on Apple Silicon)
If you are on Apple Silicon and later need `x86_64`-only software, macOS uses a
translation layer called **Rosetta 2**:
```bash
softwareupdate --install-rosetta --agree-to-license
```
`--agree-to-license` auto-accepts Apple's license. Only run it if you are
comfortable; otherwise omit the flag and accept interactively. Intel-Mac users do
**not** need Rosetta.
:::

#### File locations

There is no Windows/Linux boundary to worry about; it is all one native
filesystem. Your home directory is `~` (that is, `/Users/<your-username>`). Keep
your analysis projects anywhere convenient in your home folder.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## A note on Homebrew (optional)
Many Mac users install **Homebrew**, a general macOS package manager. It is handy
for everyday tools, **but for this series we use Conda** for bioinformatics
software, because Conda environments keep projects reproducible and isolated. You
do **not** need Homebrew to follow along.
:::

::: {.callout-warning collapse="true"}
## 🧰 Troubleshooting (macOS)
- **`xcode-select --install` says the tools are already installed** → that is
  fine, nothing to do.
- **A tool later fails to install on Apple Silicon** → see the
  [Apple Silicon note in Step 3](#apple-silicon-note); it is almost always an
  architecture (`osx-arm64` vs `osx-64`) issue, not a mistake on your part.
- **The install flow does not match** → Apple's developer-tools flow changes
  between macOS releases; check Apple's current guidance for your version.
:::

### 🐧 Linux

You already have a real Unix shell, so there is nothing to install here. Make
sure your package lists are current:

```bash
sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade -y   # Debian/Ubuntu; use your distro's manager otherwise
```

Then continue straight to **Step 2**.

:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## ✅ End of Step 1
You now have a working Unix command line. On Windows that is your Ubuntu/WSL
terminal; on macOS and Linux it is your Terminal. The rest of the module is the
same for everyone.
:::

---

## Step 2 · Install Conda (Miniforge)

You have a bench (a Unix shell). Next you need a way to fetch and organise tools
without chaos. That is Conda.

**Conda** is a package and environment manager. It lets you install scientific
software (and its dependencies) without `sudo`, and create **isolated
environments** so Project A's tools do not break Project B's.

We use **Miniforge**, a minimal, community-maintained installer that defaults to
the **conda-forge** channel. Recent Miniforge installers also include **`mamba`**,
a faster drop-in alternative to the `conda` command (anywhere you see
`conda install ...`, you can usually use `mamba install ...`).

::: {.callout-warning collapse="true"}
## ⚠️ Verify: why Miniforge and not Miniconda/Anaconda
Historically people installed Miniconda or Anaconda, which use Anaconda, Inc.'s
"defaults" channel. **Anaconda changed the terms of service** for those channels,
and some organizational or commercial uses may require a paid license. **Miniforge**
sidesteps this by defaulting to the community **conda-forge** channel. If
licensing matters for your institution, verify the *current* terms yourself; I
cannot give legal advice.
:::

#### Download and run the installer

A commonly documented one-liner auto-detects your OS and CPU architecture:

```bash
curl -L -O "https://github.com/conda-forge/miniforge/releases/latest/download/Miniforge3-$(uname)-$(uname -m).sh"
bash Miniforge3-$(uname)-$(uname -m).sh
```

Follow the prompts: page through the license and type `yes` to accept, accept the
default install location (usually `~/miniforge3`), and answer `yes` when asked to
run `conda init` so `conda` is available in new terminals.

::: {.callout-warning collapse="true"}
## ⚠️ Verify: the download URL can change
Installer filenames and available architectures are defined by the Miniforge
project. If the `curl` command returns a 404, open the official
`conda-forge/miniforge` GitHub releases page and copy the current installer link
for your system. Confirm it resolves rather than trusting the URL above blindly.
:::

#### Activate conda in your shell

Close and reopen your terminal (or run the command the installer suggests, often
`source ~/.bashrc`). You should now see `(base)` at the start of your prompt:

```
(base) amina@laptop:~$
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## ✅ Check: is conda working?
```bash
conda --version
```
Expected (version will differ):
```
conda 24.x.x
```
If instead you get "command not found", the shell init step did not run. Reopen
the terminal; if it still fails, re-run the installer's `conda init` step.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Optional: stop `(base)` auto-activating in every shell
```bash
conda config --set auto_activate_base false
```
:::

---

## Step 3 · Configure channels and build your first environment

Conda is installed. Now tell it *where* to find bioinformatics software, then
build your first environment. This is the moment the bench gets its tools.

#### What are "channels"?

Channels are the repositories Conda downloads from. Two matter for bioinformatics:

- **conda-forge**: a huge community channel of general scientific software.
- **bioconda**: the channel for bioinformatics tools (aligners, samtools, and so
  on). **Bioconda depends on conda-forge.**

#### Configure the channels

```bash
conda config --add channels bioconda
conda config --add channels conda-forge
conda config --set channel_priority strict
```

Because `--add` puts each new channel on top, the resulting priority is
**conda-forge (highest) → bioconda → everything else**, which is what Bioconda
expects. `channel_priority strict` makes dependency resolution more reliable and
faster.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## ✅ Check your channel config
```bash
conda config --show channels
```
Expected order (conda-forge above bioconda):
```
channels:
  - conda-forge
  - bioconda
```
:::

::: {.callout-warning collapse="true"}
## ⚠️ Verify: confirm the current Bioconda setup
Bioconda's recommended channel configuration has been updated over time, partly in
response to the Anaconda "defaults" licensing changes. The three commands above
reflect the common conda-forge-first pattern, but confirm the current recommended
setup on the **official Bioconda documentation** before relying on it for real
work. If later `conda install` commands cannot find packages, an out-of-date
channel config is the first thing to check.
:::

::: {.callout-important collapse="true"}
## Apple Silicon: when a Mac package "is not found" {#apple-silicon-note}
**Apple Silicon (M-series) users only.** Intel Mac, Windows, and Linux users can
skip this.

Sometimes on Apple Silicon a `conda create`/`conda install` fails with a
`PackagesNotFoundError` because the tool has an Intel-Mac build (`osx-64`) but not
yet a native Apple-Silicon build (`osx-arm64`). A common workaround is to create
an **Intel (`osx-64`) environment**, which runs through Rosetta 2:

```bash
CONDA_SUBDIR=osx-64 conda create -n bioinfo-intro fastqc samtools
conda activate bioinfo-intro
conda config --env --set subdir osx-64   # future installs in THIS env also use osx-64
```

Two honest caveats: native `osx-arm64` support keeps improving, so try the normal
command in the next section first and only fall back to this if you hit a "not
found" error; and the exact `CONDA_SUBDIR` mechanism can change between conda
versions, so confirm it in the current conda docs.
:::

#### Create your first environment

**Never install project tools into `base`.** Make a dedicated environment. This
is the labelled-bottle rule, now in practice. Create one called `bioinfo-intro`
with two classic tools: **FastQC** (quality-control reports for sequencing reads)
and **samtools** (a Swiss-army knife for sequence alignment files):

```bash
conda create -n bioinfo-intro fastqc samtools
```

`-n bioinfo-intro` names the environment; Conda shows a plan of packages, type `y`
to proceed. (Swap `conda` for `mamba` for a faster solve if Miniforge installed
it.)

::: {.callout-warning collapse="true"}
## ⚠️ Verify: pin versions for real projects
For a quick demo, installing "latest" is fine. For **reproducible** work, pin
versions (for example `fastqc=<version>`, `samtools=<version>`). I deliberately do
not hard-code numbers here because they go stale. When you build a real analysis
environment, record the exact versions you used (see Step 4).
:::

#### Activate and use the environment

```bash
conda activate bioinfo-intro
```

Your prompt should now show `(bioinfo-intro)`. Confirm the tools are available:

```bash
fastqc --version
samtools --version
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## ✅ Check
Each prints a version string, for example:
```
FastQC v0.xx.x
samtools 1.xx
```
If you get "command not found", make sure the environment is **activated** (you
should see `(bioinfo-intro)` in your prompt, not `(base)`).
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Switching and listing environments
```bash
conda deactivate         # back to base / no environment
conda activate <name>    # switch to another project
conda env list           # list all your environments
```
:::

::: {.insight}
Step back and see what you built. You did not just install two tools. You built a
sealed room, `bioinfo-intro`, put FastQC and samtools inside it, and can open and
close that room at will. Next project needs different tools? Build a different
room. They never touch each other. That isolation is the entire point, and it is
why your future self will never spend a week debugging "it worked yesterday."
:::

---

## Step 4 · Make it reproducible

This is one of the most important habits in bioinformatics. **Your analysis is
only trustworthy if someone else (including future-you) can recreate the exact
software environment.**

Export the currently active environment to a file, and recreate it anywhere:

```bash
conda env export > environment.yml          # save it
conda env create -f environment.yml         # rebuild it elsewhere
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Two flavors of export
- `conda env export` captures everything, including exact builds. Most
  reproducible, but can be OS-specific.
- `conda env export --from-history` captures only the packages *you explicitly
  asked for*. More portable across operating systems, less exact.

For teaching/portability, `--from-history` is often nicer; for locking down a
production pipeline, the full export is safer. Verify the exact flag behavior in
the current conda docs.
:::

A minimal hand-written `environment.yml` looks like this (keep one per module in
an `env/` folder):

```{.yaml filename="env/bioinfo-intro.yml"}
name: bioinfo-intro
channels:
  - conda-forge
  - bioconda
dependencies:
  - fastqc
  - samtools
  # For real work, pin versions, e.g.:
  #   - samtools=1.XX      # <-- replace with a real, current version
```

::: {.callout-warning collapse="true"}
## ⚠️ Verify
The `1.XX` above is a placeholder, **not a real version number**. Look up the
current version on the tool's official page or with `conda search samtools` before
pinning.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Optional: cleaning up
```bash
conda env remove -n bioinfo-intro   # remove an environment you no longer need
conda clean --all                   # reclaim disk space from cached downloads
```
:::

## 🚧 The mistake almost everyone makes

::: {.mistake}
Day two arrives. You are excited. You install your next tool with a quick
`conda install <tool>` while `(base)` is showing in your prompt. It works. You
move on.

Weeks later, `base` is a tangled mess of clashing versions, and something breaks
for no visible reason. This is the number-one beginner trap: **installing tools
into `base`**.

`base` is the lobby, not an office. Keep it clean. Every project gets its own
named environment. Always.
:::

## 🧩 Mini challenge

::: {.challenge}
Prof. Zola drops by: "Build me a second environment called `align-demo` with an
aligner in it, and hand me a file I can use to rebuild it exactly."

Before you read on, sketch the commands in your head.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Reveal the answer
Create the environment (verify the package name first with `conda search`),
activate it, then export it:

```bash
conda create -n align-demo bwa      # or bowtie2; confirm the name with conda search
conda activate align-demo
conda env export > env/align-demo.yml
```

Two tools, one file, fully reproducible. That is the whole habit in three lines.
:::

## 😂 Bioinformatics reality

::: {.reality}
Prof. Zola: "Did you set up your environment?"<br>
Amina: "Yes."<br>
Prof. Zola: "Can you rebuild it from scratch on a new laptop?"<br>
Amina: "...give me one minute."<br>
Prof. Zola: "That minute is the whole job."
:::

## Check yourself

Not graded. Just a quick self-test.

1. Should you install project tools into `base`, or into a named environment?
2. Which command saves an environment to a file you can rebuild it from?
3. In the channel priority order, should `conda-forge` sit above or below
   `bioconda`?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answers
1. A named environment, never `base`.
2. `conda env export > environment.yml`.
3. `conda-forge` sits *above* `bioconda`, the order Bioconda expects.
:::

## 🎯 Key takeaway

::: {.takeaway}
Setting up your bench is not the boring bit before the real work. It *is* real
work. A Unix shell, Conda, configured channels, and isolated, reproducible
environments are the quiet foundation that makes every experiment after this one
just work. Build it once, carefully, and stop fighting your own tools forever.
:::

::: {.didyouknow}
Bioconda distributes thousands of bioinformatics packages and has been used to
install software for a huge share of published sequencing studies. The moment you
ran `conda config --add channels bioconda`, you plugged into the same supply line
that countless labs around the world rely on every day.
:::

## Where to go next

You have finished the setup module, the foundation the rest of the series builds
on. If parts of this felt fiddly, that is completely normal and not a sign you
are "not a computer person." Shells and package managers are genuinely
unintuitive at first, and become second nature only with repetition.

So the most useful thing you can do now is **practise**: create a few throwaway
environments, install tools, break them, delete them, rebuild them. Muscle memory
is the whole game. And remember these tutorials are a starting point, not the
finish line. Lean on the official docs for WSL, Conda, and Bioconda whenever you
want to go deeper.

::: {.callout-important collapse="true"}
## One more time on accuracy
If any command in this module did not behave as described, the most likely reasons
are a version/OS difference, or the tool changed after this was written. Check the
official documentation for **WSL (Microsoft)**, **Miniforge (conda-forge)**,
**Conda**, and **Bioconda**. Those are the authoritative sources, and they
supersede this tutorial whenever they disagree with it.
:::
